column5: celestial lights mark seasons and years
column6: The commentary cites crescents as time markers and lunar stations for calculation; Genesis assigns the heavenly lights to seasons, days, and years, placing calendrical order in the created sky.

column5: moon for appointed times; sun's setting
column6: The commentary defines yawm by sunrise and sunset and adds lunar stations; this verse assigns the moon to appointed times and says the sun knows its setting, joining both clocks in one creation hymn.
The commentary's yawm runs from sunrise to sunset; Ecclesiastes depicts the sun rising, setting, and returning to its place, making the repeated daytime circuit explicit.
The commentary pictures the sky turning through the day; the psalm's sun runs across the heavens from one end to the other, adding a full-circuit image to the sunrise-to-sunset gloss.
The commentary's Arabic root gloss pictures the sun standing at noon; Joshua says the sun stood in mid-heaven and did not hurry to set, presenting a miraculous extension of daylight.
The commentary's gloss places the sun upright at noon with almost no shadow; Amos reverses that image by making the sun set at noon and darkening the day as a judgment sign.

The commentary says the cave's sun shifts aside from the sleepers; the psalm promises that sun will not strike by day nor moon by night under God's keeping, a close image of shelter from celestial exposure.
The commentary cites the crescent as a time marker for people and pilgrimage; the psalm sounds a trumpet at the new moon and full moon for a feast, showing lunar phases setting communal worship time.

The commentary's source gloss describes a crescent just risen above the horizon; the Mishnah has Rabban Gamliel use moon-shaped images to question witnesses, showing how visible lunar form could govern the calendar.

column5: moon phases mark seasons and festivals
column6: The commentary names lunar stations as aids to reckoning and crescents as time signs; Sirach describes the moon's phases as markers of seasons and feast days, an explicit Jewish calendrical parallel.

column5: sun shining and moon in splendor
column6: The commentary's Abraham says he does not love the setting luminaries; Job describes seeing the bright sun or moon walking in splendor, then tests whether that sight entices him to worship.
The commentary contrasts worship of the sun with worship of God alone; Job names a secretly enticed heart and a hand kissing the mouth as the gesture of astral devotion.
The commentary's Abraham turns from setting lights to the Creator of heaven and earth; Job says worship of the sun or moon would deny the God above, making the theological judgment explicit.

column5: sun, moon, and host of heaven
column6: The commentary distinguishes worship of the rising and setting lights from worship of their Creator; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to be drawn into bowing to the sun, moon, stars, or heavenly host.
The commentary cites the prohibition on prostrating to sun and moon; Deuteronomy treats serving either luminary or the host of heaven as covenantal apostasy, giving the prohibition a legal setting.

column5: men bowing to the eastern sun
column6: The commentary describes people prostrating to the sun instead of God; Ezekiel sees men with their backs to the temple and faces east, bowing to the sun, making the bodily reversal concrete.
The commentary's sun-worshippers have a public cult; Kings reports priests burning incense to the sun, moon, constellations, and all the host of heaven, supplying an Israelite institutional example.

column5: star carried as a god's image
column6: The commentary's Abraham sees a star and rejects a setting object as lord; WLC Amos names a star of a god among Israel's cult objects, showing the same kind of celestial body made an object of worship.
The commentary says sun-worship kept a people from the path; Stephen says God turned away and gave Israel over to worship the host of heaven, linking astral worship with divine abandonment.

The commentary's Abraham refuses a celestial body as lord; Stephen revoices the star-god tradition of Amos as the star of Rephan and connects the cult to exile, showing a Christian reception of Israel's astral-idolatry text.

The commentary rejects worship of sun and moon and turns to their Creator; Wisdom says people may take sun, moon, and stars for gods because of their beauty, but should recognize their Lord as greater because he made them.

The commentary ends Abraham's sky scene with his face turned to the Creator of heaven and earth; in Genesis Abraham swears by the Most High, maker of heaven and earth, giving a close Abrahamic statement of allegiance.

column4: Jacob of Serugh, Homily on the Young Men of Ephesus
column6: The commentary describes young sleepers sheltered in a cave; Jacob's Syriac homily recounts the Christian youths of Ephesus sleeping in a cave, a close narrative parallel, while the Qur'anic commentary singles out the sun's path around them.
The commentary's root gloss evokes a high, unobscured midday sun; Mark places darkness over the land from the sixth hour, a contrary noon image in a distinct scene.

The commentary links the straight-path image to the sun at its noon height; Proverbs pictures the righteous path as dawn light growing brighter until full day, joining ethical direction to the day's light.
The commentary's source gloss describes the sky as what is above and shades a person; this psalm calls the LORD one's shade at the right hand, transferring the shelter image to divine protection.

The commentary evokes a crescent and a station of the moon; 1 Enoch lays out the moon's recurring phases and course, giving a Jewish astronomical account of the ordered lunar cycle without equating its system with the commentary's term.

The commentary cites lunar stations for counting years and crescents for marking times; Jubilees prescribes a 364-day year and warns against lunar reckoning that disrupts the seasons, a specific Jewish calendar counter-position.

column5: horses and chariots for the sun
column6: The commentary names the sun as an object people worship; Kings reports solar horses and chariots at the temple entrance, a distinct royal rite removed by Josiah.

The commentary's Abraham tests a star, moon, and sun and turns to their Creator; Jubilees presents Abram studying celestial signs before recognizing sun, moon, and stars as subject to the Lord, a related Abraham tradition whose concern is prognostication rather than a sequence of rival lords.

column5: stars as a promise, not lords
column6: The commentary's Abraham treats a star's setting as grounds not to love it; Genesis directs Abraham to count the stars as a sign of promised descendants, giving the same celestial gaze a promise-bearing rather than devotional role.

The commentary's Abraham seeks guidance after the moon sets and turns to the Creator; Genesis says Abraham believes the LORD in the star-promise scene, placing trust in God rather than in the lights themselves.
The commentary mentions a woman ruling the sun-worshipping people; Kings introduces the Queen of Sheba coming to Solomon, a matching royal setting for the Qur'anic report.

The commentary places a female ruler over a sun-worshipping people; in Kings the Queen of Sheba blesses the LORD for establishing Solomon, so the parallel foregrounds different religious emphases in the two Sheba accounts.

The commentary's command rejects prostration to sun and moon in favor of their Creator; Paul names the same creator-creature reversal in describing people who worship and serve what was made, though he does not specify the luminaries.

The commentary treats the crescent and lunar stations as useful measures of time; Paul places observance of days, months, seasons, and years within the Galatians' return to bondage, a contrasting Christian evaluation, though he does not name the crescent.

column5: Father of lights without turning's shadow
column6: The commentary's image makes the sun, moon, and sky change position and cast or lose shadows; James calls God the Father of lights with no variation or shadow from turning, a specific image-level contrast between changing lights and God.

column5: greater and lesser lights govern day and night
column6: The commentary's command rejects prostration to sun and moon because they are created; Genesis says God made the greater and lesser lights to govern day and night, supplying the creation order behind their demotion from gods.

column5: sunrise and the creatures' daily cycle
column6: The commentary defines yawm by the sun's course from sunrise to sunset; this verse says the sun rises and nocturnal animals return to their dens, showing the daily transition.
The commentary's yawm spans sunrise to sunset; the next verse places human labor between sunrise and evening, giving that span a human daily rhythm.
The commentary joins the turning daylight to Fatiha's praise of God; this psalm says the LORD's name is praised from the sun's rising to its setting, making worship fill the same solar interval.

column5: God's name great from sunrise to sunset
column6: The commentary separates worship of the sun from worship of God; Malachi says God's name is great among the nations from the sun's rising to its setting and that incense is offered to him everywhere.

column5: sun and moon praise the LORD
column6: The commentary says people must worship the Creator rather than the sun and moon; the psalm calls those same luminaries to praise the LORD, reversing the direction of worship.
The commentary's solar prohibition directs worship to the one who made the luminaries; Nehemiah's prayer says the host of heaven worships the God who made heaven and all its host.

column5: divine light and truth lead the speaker
column6: The commentary's Abraham fears becoming astray without the Lord's guidance and turns from transient lights; the psalm asks God's light and truth to lead the speaker to God's altar, making divine illumination a guide rather than an object of worship.

column5: God appoints sun, moon, and stars
column6: The commentary presents the sky's daily and lunar motions as a created order; Jeremiah names God as the one who gives the sun for daytime light and appoints the moon and stars by night.

column5: sun's rising and heat at noon
column6: The commentary's source gloss describes the sun standing at noon with little shadow; Sirach praises the sun at its rising and its powerful heat at noon, giving a Jewish description of the same daily solar arc.

The commentary pictures the sky turning through the day from sunrise to sunset; the Astronomical Book describes the sun's ordered rising and setting through heavenly gates, an expanded Jewish account of the solar course.

column5: straying from the way as light and sun fail
column6: The commentary joins Abraham's fear of being astray with the setting of celestial lights; Wisdom's condemned speakers say they strayed from the way of truth, that righteousness's light did not shine, and that the sun did not rise for them.

column5: YHWH replaces sun and moon as light
column6: The commentary calls sun and moon created lights that must not receive worship; Isaiah says restored Zion will no longer need the sun by day or moon by night because YHWH will be its everlasting light.

The commentary directs worship from sun and moon to their Creator; Revelation's city needs neither because God's glory illuminates it and the Lamb is its lamp, carrying Isaiah's contrast into a Christian vision.

column5: light guides feet to the way of peace
column6: The commentary's Abraham asks for guidance away from error and the Fatiha asks for the straight path; Zechariah's song has dawn-light reach those in darkness and guide their feet to peace.

The commentary's Abraham watches star, moon, and sun before turning to the Creator; Genesis Rabbah reads God's instruction to look at the stars as answering Abram's astrological forecast that he would have no child, a Jewish interpretation that subordinates celestial fate to divine guidance.

column5: sun darkened before the day of the LORD
column6: The commentary defines the day under the sun's ordinary rise and setting; in WLC numbering Joel places the sun's darkening and moon's change before the great day of the LORD, joining celestial reversal to a day of judgment.

The commentary presents the crescent as a marker for communal time and pilgrimage; Colossians names festivals and new moons among observances over which Christians should not be judged, a different religious framing of lunar time.
The commentary's image follows celestial lights rising over the horizon; Zechariah's song names a dawn from on high visiting the people, using sunrise as an image of divine arrival.

column5: star leads the travelers and stands over the child
column6: The commentary's Abraham sees a star and rejects it as lord when it sets; Matthew's star serves as a sign that leads the travelers to the child, giving the celestial object a guiding rather than divine role.

column5: worship directed to the child, not the star
column6: The commentary distinguishes worship of God from worship of celestial lights; after the star guides them, the Magi fall down before the child, so the narrative directs prostration away from the star.

column5: sun and moon darkened at the coming of the Son of Man
column6: The commentary places the day of judgment alongside the ordinary solar day; Matthew describes sun and moon losing their light and stars falling before the Son of Man, giving a Christian apocalyptic meeting of judgment and celestial signs.

column5: the sun's light fails at the sixth hour
column6: The commentary's root gloss pictures the sun standing high at noon; Luke says the sun's light failed during the darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour, a distinct Christian noon reversal.

column5: shadow moves backward as a solar sign
column6: The commentary's source gloss pictures noon with the shadow nearly absent; Hezekiah asks for the shadow to move backward on the steps, using the sun-shadow relation as a miraculous sign rather than a stable midday balance.

The commentary's source glossary calls al-na'im one lunar mansion; Job names Mazzaroth in its season among celestial groups, a possible parallel in ordered sky stations, though the identity of Mazzaroth and its relation to lunar mansions are uncertain.
